items.stem: Chloé writes: "The Cold War began suddenly in 1947 with the Truman Doctrine." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Tensions developed from 1943–45 over Poland, the second front and post-war aims, and intensified in 1946 (Long Telegram, Iron Curtain speech, Iran crisis) before the Truman Doctrine.

items.stem: Distinguish between the Potsdam Conference and the Yalta Conference.
items.answer: Yalta (February 1945) was relatively cooperative, with agreements on Germany, the UN and Japan; Potsdam (July 1945) was more tense, with Truman replacing Roosevelt, disputes over reparations and Poland, and the atomic bomb altering the balance.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Iran crisis (1946) and explain what it reveals about the growth of mistrust in the early Cold War.
items.answer: Soviet troops remained in northern Iran beyond the agreed deadline of March 1946 and supported separatist regimes in Azerbaijan and Kurdistan before withdrawing under US and UN pressure. The USA saw the crisis as a test of Soviet expansionism, contributing to the hardening of US policy in 1946.

items.stem: Briefly explain why ideological differences made post-war cooperation difficult.
items.answer: Capitalism and liberal democracy versus Marxism–Leninism implied rival visions of the post-war world: the USA sought open markets and self-determination, the USSR believed conflict with capitalism was inevitable and sought security through communist regimes.

items.stem: Explain why the atomic bomb increased mistrust between the USA and the USSR.
items.answer: Truman told Stalin of a powerful new weapon at Potsdam but did not share it; Soviet leaders saw the bomb as a means of atomic diplomacy aimed at them, and accelerated their own programme, which tested a bomb in August 1949.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "salami tactics"?

The gradual elimination of non-communist parties in Eastern Europe, “slice by slice”, a term associated with the Hungarian communist leader Mátyás Rákosi
The North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a military alliance of twelve Western states founded in April 1949, whose Article 5 treats an attack on one as an attack on all

items.stem: Mei writes: "The Marshall Plan was offered only to Western European countries." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It was offered to all European countries, including the USSR and Eastern Europe, but Stalin refused and forced his satellites to decline.

items.stem: Explain why Stalin established communist control in Eastern Europe.
items.answer: He wanted a buffer zone against invasion from the west, reparations and resources for reconstruction, and believed in spreading socialism; Western policies such as the Marshall Plan increased his determination to tighten control.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Truman Doctrine"?

items.stem: Using the Greek Civil War (1946–1949) as an example, explain containment in practice.
items.answer: Communist guerrillas fought the British-backed monarchy; after Britain withdrew aid in 1947 the USA took over under the Truman Doctrine and the government won by 1949. US military and economic aid prevented a communist victory, showing containment applied through support of local forces; Stalin largely respected the percentages agreement.

items.answer: The airlift kept West Berlin supplied through the winter, Stalin did not risk shooting down aircraft, the counter-blockade hurt the Soviet zone, and the crisis strengthened Western unity, leading to NATO.

items.stem: Distinguish between the Berlin Airlift and the Berlin Blockade.
items.answer: The Blockade was Stalin’s closure of land and water access to West Berlin; the Airlift was the Western response of supplying the city by air, which avoided armed confrontation.
items.markingKey: The Blockade was Stalin’s closure of land and water access to West Berlin; the Airlift was the Western response of supplying the city by air, which avoided armed confrontation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Leila writes: "Historiography is only about which side was to blame." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Interpretations also differ on causes (ideology, security, economics, personalities), on the timing of the origins and on the role of other states.
items.markingKey: Interpretations also differ on causes (ideology, security, economics, personalities), on the timing of the origins and on the role of other states. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Leila writes: "At Yalta Roosevelt and Churchill handed Eastern Europe to Stalin." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Yalta recognised the reality of Soviet military occupation but included the Declaration on Liberated Europe promising free elections; the division resulted from Soviet actions after 1945 rather than a formal agreement at Yalta.
items.markingKey: Yalta recognised the reality of Soviet military occupation but included the Declaration on Liberated Europe promising free elections; the division resulted from Soviet actions after 1945 rather than a formal agreement at Yalta. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan.
items.answer: The Truman Doctrine was a political and military commitment to support governments resisting communism, beginning with Greece and Turkey; the Marshall Plan was economic aid to rebuild Europe and remove the conditions in which communism might spread.
items.markingKey: The Truman Doctrine was a political and military commitment to support governments resisting communism, beginning with Greece and Turkey; the Marshall Plan was economic aid to rebuild Europe and remove the conditions in which communism might spread. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "The Berlin Blockade led directly to war between the superpowers." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Neither side fired on the other; the crisis was resolved without fighting when Stalin lifted the Blockade in May 1949.
items.markingKey: Neither side fired on the other; the crisis was resolved without fighting when Stalin lifted the Blockade in May 1949. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Vladislav Zubok and Constantine Pleshakov, Inside the Kremlin’s Cold War (1996) as an example, explain the impact of new evidence on Cold War historiography.
items.answer: Using Soviet archives they described a “revolutionary-imperial paradigm” combining security concerns with ideological expansion. Their work showed that new sources can complicate earlier interpretations rather than simply confirming one side.
items.markingKey: Context (Using Soviet archives they described a “revolutionary-imperial paradigm” combining security concerns with ideological expansion.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Their work showed that new sources can complicate earlier interpretations rather than simply confirming one side. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the impact of new evidence on Cold War historiography.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Iran crisis (1946) shows the growth of mistrust in the early Cold War.
items.answer: Soviet troops remained in northern Iran beyond the agreed deadline of March 1946 and supported separatist regimes in Azerbaijan and Kurdistan before withdrawing under US and UN pressure. The USA saw the crisis as a test of Soviet expansionism, contributing to the hardening of US policy in 1946.
items.markingKey: Context (Soviet troops remained in northern Iran beyond the agreed deadline of March 1946 and supported separatist regimes in Azerbaijan and Kurdistan before withdrawing under US and UN pressure.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem:
Source D
[Cartoon] A Soviet cartoon shows Uncle Sam with a bag of dollars labelled “Marshall Plan”, holding a leash attached to collars around the necks of figures labelled “France”, “Italy” and “Britain”.
— Description of a cartoon from the Soviet satirical magazine Krokodil, 1948

With reference to the origin, purpose and content of Source D, assess its values and limitations for historians investigating Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe and US containment, 1945–1949. [4]
items.answer: Value: It shows the official Soviet interpretation of the Marshall Plan presented to Soviet citizens. Limitations: Krokodil was a state-controlled publication; the cartoon is propaganda reflecting the party line rather than evidence of the plan’s effects.
items.markingKey: Value: It shows the official Soviet interpretation of the Marshall Plan presented to Soviet citizens. Limitations: Krokodil was a state-controlled publication; the cartoon is propaganda reflecting the party line rather than evidence of the plan’s effects. items.stem:
Source B
The Western powers have violated the Potsdam decisions by carrying out a separate currency reform and preparing a separate West German government. The measures taken on the communications with Berlin are necessary to protect the economy of the Soviet zone from the disruption caused by the new currency.
— Soviet note to the Western powers, July 1948 (paraphrased)

What, according to Source B, were the main features of the Berlin Blockade and the division of Germany? [3]
items.answer: The West had broken Potsdam through separate currency reform and plans for a West German state; Soviet restrictions on Berlin were defensive; they protected the Soviet zone economy.
items.markingKey: The West had broken Potsdam through separate currency reform and plans for a West German state; Soviet restrictions on Berlin were defensive; they protected the Soviet zone economy. Award 1 mark for each relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]. Points must be taken from the source; own knowledge is not credited in Question 1.

items.stem:
Source A
At the bottom of the Kremlin’s neurotic view of world affairs is the traditional and instinctive Russian sense of insecurity. Soviet power is impervious to the logic of reason, but it is highly sensitive to the logic of force. For this reason it can easily withdraw – and usually does – when strong resistance is encountered at any point.
— George F. Kennan, US chargé d’affaires in Moscow, the “Long Telegram” to the State Department, 22 February 1946 (extract)

With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source A for an historian studying the origins of the Cold War, 1943–1946. [4]
items.answer: Value: Written by an experienced diplomat and Russia specialist in Moscow, it was highly influential, providing the intellectual basis for containment. Limitations: It was intended to persuade Washington to adopt a tougher line; it is a generalised interpretation that Kennan later said had been misread as calling for military containment.
items.markingKey: Value: Written by an experienced diplomat and Russia specialist in Moscow, it was highly influential, providing the intellectual basis for containment. items.stem: Evaluate the reasons for the Soviet takeover of Eastern Europe between 1945 and 1949. [15]
items.answer: Security was Stalin’s primary motive, but ideology determined the form of control and Western policy accelerated it.
items.markingKey: Paper 3 essay. Indicative content: security buffer; ideology and Cominform; presence of the Red Army; response to the Marshall Plan. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Security was Stalin’s primary motive, but ideology determined the form of control and Western policy accelerated it. items.stem: "The Berlin Blockade was a turning point in the early Cold War." Discuss.
items.answer: The Blockade turned an emerging division into an institutional one, but it built on processes already under way.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: led to NATO and the FRG and GDR in 1949; first direct superpower confrontation; confirmed the division of Germany. Arguments against: the division of Germany was already under way (Bizonia, currency reform); the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan were earlier turning points; the Korean War militarised the Cold War more. Supported judgement: The Blockade turned an emerging division into an institutional one, but it built on processes already under way. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The meeting of Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin in the Crimea in February 1945 that agreed on the zones of occupation in Germany, free elections in liberated Europe (the Declaration on Liberated Europe) and Soviet entry into the war against Japan"?
options: Berlin Airlift
NATO
Yalta Conference
revisionist interpretation
items.answer: Yalta Conference
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of Yalta Conference.

items.stem: Define the term "salami tactics".
items.answer: The gradual elimination of non-communist parties in Eastern Europe, “slice by slice”, a term associated with the Hungarian communist leader Mátyás Rákosi
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the gradual elimination of non-communist parties in Eastern Europe, “slice by slice”, a term associated with the Hungarian communist leader Mátyás Rákosi. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims that NATO was formed after the Korean War began. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: NATO was founded in April 1949, before the Korean War (June 1950), although the war led to its military integration and later West German rearmament.
items.markingKey: NATO was founded in April 1949, before the Korean War (June 1950), although the war led to its military integration and later West German rearmament. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the orthodox interpretation and the revisionist interpretation.
items.answer: Orthodox historians blamed Soviet expansionism and saw US policy as a defensive response; revisionists blamed US economic expansionism, atomic diplomacy and refusal to accept Soviet security needs.
items.markingKey: Orthodox historians blamed Soviet expansionism and saw US policy as a defensive response; revisionists blamed US economic expansionism, atomic diplomacy and refusal to accept Soviet security needs. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the issue of Poland caused tension between the Allies in 1945.
items.answer: Britain had gone to war over Poland and backed the London Poles, while Stalin installed the communist Lublin Committee; Yalta’s vague promise of “free elections” was interpreted differently, and Soviet arrests of Home Army leaders convinced the West that Stalin was breaking agreements.

(2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "Post-revisionist historians argue that neither side bore any responsibility for the Cold War." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Post-revisionists argue that both sides shared responsibility through misperception and the security dilemma, not that neither was responsible.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Novikov Telegram (September 1946) and explain what it reveals about mutual misperception as a cause of the Cold War.
items.answer: The Soviet ambassador in Washington, Nikolai Novikov, reported that the USA sought world supremacy and was preparing for war with the USSR. Mirroring Kennan’s Long Telegram, it shows that each side interpreted the other’s actions as aggressive.
items.markingKey: Context (The Soviet ambassador in Washington, Nikolai Novikov, reported that the USA sought world supremacy and was preparing for war with the USSR.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Briefly describe the Czech coup (February 1948) and explain what it reveals about Soviet consolidation of control in Eastern Europe.
items.answer: The communists, led by Klement Gottwald, took full power after non-communist ministers resigned; elections in May offered only a single list. The coup removed the last democracy in Eastern Europe and convinced Congress to pass the Marshall Plan in April 1948.
items.markingKey: Context (The communists, led by Klement Gottwald, took full power after non-communist ministers resigned; elections in May offered only a single list.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Briefly describe the North Atlantic Treaty (4 April 1949) and explain what it reveals about the institutionalisation of the Cold War.
items.answer: Twelve states including the USA, Canada, Britain and France signed the treaty in Washington. For the first time the USA entered a peacetime military alliance, formalising its commitment to defend Western Europe.
items.markingKey: Context (Twelve states including the USA, Canada, Britain and France signed the treaty in Washington.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Source B
The Cold War was the product of a Soviet drive for expansion. The United States, after trying to cooperate, responded reluctantly with a policy of containment.
— Summary of the orthodox view, based on Herbert Feis, Churchill, Roosevelt, Stalin (1957) (paraphrased)

Outline the message that the author of Source B intended to convey. [2]
items.answer: The Cold War resulted from Soviet expansion; the USA initially sought cooperation; containment was a reluctant response.

items.answer: Ideology framed each side’s perception of the other, but specific security disputes in 1945–47 turned mistrust into conflict.
